chunks: And as for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Kazzaz from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim from Ja'far from his father from Ali (peace be upon him)
In the case of a man who performed الظهار (Zihar) with four women, he said: 'Upon him is one expiation.'
This is to be understood as meaning one expiation in kind, either freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people.
And it is not obligatory for some of them to have their slave freed, and for others fasting or feeding.
And the meaning of his saying 'one expiation' is not that one of these expiations suffices for the four women.
And whoever performs Zihar with one woman many times, upon him is for the number of each time an expiation.
That is indicated by what he narrated:

key_terms.إِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِيناً: Feeding sixty poor people, the third option if unable to fast.
key_terms.صِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ: Fasting two consecutive months, the second option if unable to free a slave.
key_terms.ظَاهَرَ: Zihar, a form of pre-Islamic and Islamic conjugal separation where a husband declares his wife like his mother's back.
key_terms.عِتْقُ رَقَبَةٍ: Freeing a slave, the first option in the hierarchy of expiation.
key_terms.كَفَّارَةٌ: Expiation, the penalty required to lift the prohibition of Zihar.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of Zihar with multiple wives in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that the phrase 'one expiation' refers to the type of expiation (e.g., freeing a slave, fasting, or feeding) rather than a single act covering multiple wives, meaning each wife requires a distinct expiation. This interpretation aligns with the principle that repeated Zihar with a single wife also incurs separate expiations, emphasizing the individuality of the marital bond in this legal context. The ruling underscores the seriousness of Zihar as a distinct form of conjugal separation requiring specific atonement.
